To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have found that 6.8 percent of young patients with second malignant neoplasm carry inherited mutations in the p-53 tumor-suppressor genes.
germline mutations of p53 were identified in the blood leukocytes from four of 59 (6.8%) patients with second primary cancers.
germline mutations of p53 are associated with second cancers in some children and young adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis of cancer in children.
the molecular genetic basis of cancer, and in particular, the identification of genetic alterations that are associated with the development of human cancers.
understanding the genetic mechanisms underlying cancer in humans, and how this information can be applied in the clinical setting to improve the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no such thing as a “second” primary cancer.
the p53 tumor suppressor gene is a major determinant of the susceptibility to a variety of cancers in humans.
the p53 gene mutations are not the cause of the second primary cancer in the patients, but they are associated with an increased risk of the development of a second primary cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the p53 tumor suppressor gene plays an important role in the development of cancer.

the p53 gene plays an important role in the genesis of second cancers in childhood and early adulthood and that germline mutations of this gene may be a common cause of these tumors. (N Engl J Med 1992;326:1301-5.)
we identified a group of patients with second malignant neoplasm that were not associated with the Li-Fraumi syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a subgroup of children and young adults whose second primary cancers are associated with germline p53 mutations.
the Li-Fraumani syndrome is not the only genetic condition that predisposes to cancer in young people.
there are many families with germline p53 mutations that do not meet the classic criteria for Li-Fraumenie families.
